scenes.visual: Title card: Two Detectors of Change. Keep silent 3.0 s.

scenes.tts: Slide a fingertip across cloth, or hold a buzzing phone. Two kinds of touch organ answer. Mice-ner corpuscles report flutter and movement across the skin. Pa-sin-ee-an corpuscles report the fast hum of vibration. Both fire when contact changes, and go quiet during a steady press. And neither is just a nerve ending. Each is a nerve ending wrapped in cells that help it feel.
scenes.visual: Fingertip over a skin cross-section; a small Meissner corpuscle near the surface lights on a slow wave, a deep Pacinian corpuscle lights on a fast wave; sketch spikes at onset and offset only (in this sketch); label 'two detectors of change'.

scenes.tts: How do we know they split the work? In nineteen sixty-eight, Talbot, Mountcastle and colleagues vibrated people's hands. From about five to forty hertz, it felt like a light flutter. From around sixty to eighty hertz upward, it felt like a deeper hum. The same study recorded single nerve fibres in monkeys. Flutter matched fibres now tied to Mice-ner corpuscles. The hum matched Pa-sin-ee-an fibres. And in mice, behavioural sensitivity peaks at a higher frequency than in people.
scenes.visual: Frequency axis with a 'flutter' band and a 'hum' band; human and monkey icons kept visibly separate; two afferent sketch traces under the bands; a human and a mouse sensitivity peak, the mouse peak further right (in this sketch).
scenes.narration: How do we know they split the work? In 1968, Talbot, Mountcastle and colleagues vibrated people's hands. From about 5 to 40 Hz, it felt like a light flutter. From around 60 to 80 Hz upward, it felt like a deeper hum. The same study recorded single nerve fibres in monkeys. Flutter matched fibres now tied to Meissner corpuscles. The hum matched Pacinian fibres. And in mice, behavioural sensitivity peaks at a higher frequency than in people.

scenes.tts: Where does force become current? In mice, the answer starts in the axon. A channel called Pee-ay-zo two sits in the sensory axon membrane, out to tiny protrusions tethered to the wrapping cells. Without it, light touch is almost lost. Delete it from the wrapping cells alone, and touch responses stay. A press stretches the axon, the channels open, and the current drives spikes.
scenes.visual: Close-up of a terminal with short protrusions anchored to lamellar cells; channel icons on the axon membrane open as it stretches; a current arrow, then spikes.

scenes.tts: But the wrapping cells are not just padding. In duck bill corpuscles, these flattened lamellar cells respond to force themselves, and depolarizing one can make its nerve fibre fire. In mice, switching Pa-sin-ee-an lamellar cells on with light drove the fibre. Switching them off made vibration about five times harder to detect. How these cells signal to the nerve ending is still unknown.
scenes.visual: Lamellar cells around a terminal; one lights up and a spike follows (chip: 'duck'); a mouse paw with a threshold bar rising about fivefold when the cells are switched off (chip: 'mouse'); a question mark on the gap between cell and terminal.

scenes.tts: Why is the response so brief? The classic answer was the onion of layers, a filter that soaks up slow presses. In nineteen sixty-five, Low-en-stine and Mendel-son stripped most layers from cat corpuscles. The ending's voltage then lasted longer, mainly under intense compression, yet it still fired a single spike. So brevity has two stages: mechanics around the ending, and the spike-generating membrane. In twenty twenty-five, in duck corpuscles, removing the outer layers left the terminal's fast current and tuning intact.
scenes.visual: Layers peel away; sketch traces: generator potential lasting longer, one spike; two stage labels; then a duck Herbst corpuscle with the outer core removed and a fast current sketch that stays; chip 'duck, ex vivo'.
scenes.narration: Why is the response so brief? The classic answer was the onion of layers, a filter that soaks up slow presses. In 1965, Loewenstein and Mendelson stripped most layers from cat corpuscles. The ending's voltage then lasted longer, mainly under intense compression, yet it still fired a single spike. So brevity has two stages: mechanics around the ending, and the spike-generating membrane. In 2025, in duck bill skin from late embryos, ex vivo, removing the outer layers left the terminal's fast current and tuning intact. That does not show the capsule does nothing in a cat or a human hand.

scenes.tts: Mice-ner corpuscles hold a surprise too. In mice, most hold two genetically different nerve fibres, one more sensitive than the other. Mice that grew up without Mice-ner corpuscles needed about twice the push to detect a touch. In freely moving mice, the most sensitive Pa-sin-ee-an neurons even answered taps on a branch two and a half metres away. Two detectors of change, each a nerve ending and the cells that help it feel.
scenes.visual: Meissner corpuscle with two coloured axons; a threshold bar doubling; a mouse on a branch with a tap 2.5 m away and a sketch spike train; the closing frame repeats the two-detector picture from s01.
